feedback: If the slid copy lands on the lower cluster (within tracing accuracy), the translation shows that corresponding angles are equal; then use vertically opposite angles to explain why alternate angles are equal too.
If a pupil relies on the 'F'/'Z' look, ask them to describe what MOVEMENT maps one angle onto the other, so the reason is the translation, not the letter shape.
When the lines are not parallel, point out that the copy no longer fits and the readings diverge — this is the evidence that parallelism is the condition for the equalities.
activities.intendedInsight: Corresponding angles are equal because one crossing's angle cluster can be translated along the transversal onto the other, which is a transformation, not a shape to recognise. Alternate angles are then equal because each one is vertically opposite a corresponding partner. These equalities break when the lines are not parallel.
learnerActions: Draw (or use a prepared diagram of) two parallel lines crossed by a transversal, marking the parallels with matching arrows.
Trace the four-angle cluster at the upper crossing onto tracing paper, then slide the tracing straight down along the transversal until it lands on the lower crossing.

Observe that every angle in the slid copy lands on the matching angle at the lower crossing (as closely as tracing allows; in the ideal diagram the fit is exact). State which pairs this shows are equal: corresponding angles directly, and alternate angles by combining this with vertically opposite angles at the same crossing.
Now draw a second diagram where one line is deliberately NOT parallel to the other; trace and slide again, and record where the copy fails to fit and how the readings differ.
Write a one-sentence conclusion: equality of these angle pairs depends on the lines being parallel.
activities.title: Translate the angle cluster along the transversal

feedback: If a pupil labels the co-interior angle 70°, ask them to check it against a straight line: the co-interior angle and the adjacent equal angle together make 180°, so it must be 110°.
Correct colouring with the 70°/110° split visible shows the two families are being kept apart — exactly the distinction the over-general rule erases.
activities.intendedInsight: Not all angles made with parallel lines are equal: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, while co-interior angles are supplementary, so a 70° angle produces both 70° partners and a 110° partner.
learnerActions: In a given parallel-lines-and-transversal diagram, point to one marked angle (e.g. 70°) and name its corresponding, alternate, and co-interior partners.
Colour the equal family (corresponding and alternate) in one hue and the supplementary family (co-interior) in another.
For a 70° starting angle, label each partner with its value: the equal partners read 70°, and the co-interior partner reads 110° because co-interior angles sum to 180° (180 − 70 = 110).
Explain in words why the co-interior angle is 110° and not 70°, referring to the straight line or to the equal angle that sits on a straight line with it.
activities.title: Sort angle pairs into equal and supplementary families

feedback: If a pupil says the rules 'don't apply because the lines don't look parallel', redirect them to the arrow marks: matching arrows mean parallel, so the rules do apply.
If a pupil applies equality to an unmarked, non-parallel diagram, point out there is no parallel condition shown, so the equalities are not guaranteed.
activities.intendedInsight: Parallelism is judged by the marking arrows and definition, not by how similar the lines look; the angle relationships hold in rotated and off-set diagrams whenever the lines are genuinely parallel, and must not be assumed when they are not.
learnerActions: Work with diagrams where the parallel lines overlap only a little, are off-set, or are rotated away from the usual horizontal layout, with the parallels marked by arrows.
Before applying any rule, check the arrow marks to confirm the lines really are parallel.
Pick out and name each requested angle pair (corresponding, alternate, co-interior) despite the unusual orientation.
Also examine a diagram whose lines are NOT marked parallel and explain why the equal/supplementary rules may not apply there.
activities.title: Identify pairs in off-set and rotated diagrams

feedback: Accept an answer only when each step carries a correct, precise reason; 'because of the F shape' is not a reason — name the relationship.
If a step is unjustified or a basic fact is misused, isolate that step and ask which angle fact licenses it before continuing.
activities.intendedInsight: Unknown angles are found by chaining relationships, each justified by a stated reason, building on secure basic angle facts rather than by pattern-matching a letter shape.
learnerActions: Given a diagram combining parallel lines, a transversal, and other lines, find an unknown angle that requires two or more steps.
At each step, write the angle fact used as a full reason, e.g. 'x = 45° because alternate angles are equal' or 'y = 180 − 45 = 135° because angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Use secure basic facts where needed: angles on a straight line sum to 180°, vertically opposite angles are equal, and angles at a point sum to 360°.
Check the final answer by an independent route (e.g. a different pair of angles) where possible.
activities.title: Multi-step angle chase with a stated reason at each step
